verdicts.strongest_argument: The numbers are correct — I verified 20.2 GWh, 18 GWh utility-scale, 1.8 GWh C&I, and the raise to 71 GWh vs 59 GWh in 2025 in the cited ess-news piece, sourced to the SEIA/Benchmark Q3 2026 Energy Storage Market Outlook. But the claim's headline overstates the ABM-relevant portion by roughly an order of magnitude. ~89% of the record is utility-scale, where ABM/RavenVolt is not a participant; ABM's BESS work is behind-the-meter C&I microgrid, and the same article notes H1 C&I was 'tracking 13% below 2025's total annual deployment' — the segment ABM actually serves is not the record. More decisively, the ABM-specific implication is already management's own published narrative: on 2026-06-05 ABM reported ATS revenue of $267.3m (+27%), said it 'had a really good quarter on the battery energy storage side', announced a major big-box microgrid win, called BESS 'a multiyear growth cycle', and reaffirmed FY26 revenue growth at the top of 4-5% on exactly this driver — and the stock rose 6.67% that day. National install statistics for May-June cannot inform ABM's fiscal Q3 revenue independently of a backlog ABM already described. Finally the sign is ambiguous against consensus: the preview consensus is EPS $1.04 and the whole debate is margin recovery, while management explicitly said these equipment-heavy BESS projects carry compressed margins. A record install quarter is a revenue tailwind and a mix headwind, which is not the trade the claim implies. ATS is 11.5% of revenue.

prior_publication.what_it_says: US installed a record 20.2 GWh in Q2 2026 (18 GWh utility-scale, 1.8 GWh C&I, 0.657 GWh residential); SEIA/Benchmark raised the 2026 forecast to 71 GWh, 20% above 2025's 59 GWh, while noting H1 C&I ran 13% below 2025's full-year C&I total.

ABM management reported ATS at $267.3m (+27%), described a strong battery-energy-storage quarter and a new big-box microgrid award, guided a multiyear ATS growth cycle, and flagged that near-term BESS projects carry compressed margins because they are equipment-heavy.
ABM reaffirmed FY26 adjusted EPS of $3.85-$4.15 and guided revenue growth to the top of its ranges with Technical Solutions named as the growth driver.

verdicts.baseline_evidence: The 2026-06-05 reaction was +6.67%, the largest up-move in the seven-event history, on a print whose stated driver was ATS/battery storage — the market has already paid for this narrative once. Since then spot has drifted -3.07% over 20 days with 15.1% realised vol; there is no visible re-rating on 2026-09-01 when the SEIA/Benchmark data landed, which is the one point in the claim's favour. The 8.13% implied move is not evidence either way: 93 contracts of front-expiry OI and a 78%-of-mid ATM spread make the chain indicative only.
verdicts.what_would_change_it: A disclosure that ABM's BESS revenue is materially utility-scale rather than behind-the-meter C&I, or a company datapoint sizing BESS as more than ~5% of revenue, would make the national install record transmit directly instead of through an already-guided backlog.

verdicts.strongest_argument: Every figure is right — I confirmed 18.3% vacancy, -30bp, 'the largest quarterly decline since 2015', 12.6m sq ft net absorption and ninth straight positive quarter, leasing +16% y/y to 62.4m sq ft, the projection to surpass 2022, and San Francisco's +963,980 sq ft in CBRE's separate SF Office Figures Q2 2026. Credit for accuracy. Two problems remain. First, publication: CBRE's quarterly US office figures are a staple read for anyone covering facility services, they went out 2026-07-29, and the trade press picked them up — Facilities Dive on 2026-08-04, ULI, and GlobeSt on the San Francisco tech-demand angle on 2026-09-02. Second and larger, the 'gotcha' against the CEO does not land: CBRE's own SF report puts SF vacancy at 29.2%, which still makes the CEO's 2026-06-05 'probably 2 or 3x worse than New York City' true, and he had already told the market on that same call that national net absorption 'turned significantly positive' and was 'the strongest since 2020' with prime vacancy tightening. The direction of travel is in the company's published narrative. Third, transmission barely reaches this print: 12.6m sq ft is ~0.2% of US office stock, and absorption converts to janitorial scope only after build-out and move-in, two to four quarters later — leases signed in calendar Q2 do not touch May-July revenue. Against that, B&I was flat in Q2 and management guided it to 'moderate' on client exits with TfL alone a ~300bp headwind, a company-specific offset that swamps a 30bp national vacancy improvement.

prior_publication.what_it_says: US office vacancy fell 30bp to 18.3%, the largest quarterly decline since 2015, on 12.6m sq ft of net absorption and leasing +16% y/y to 62.4m sq ft, with 2026 leasing projected to surpass the 2022 record.
Facilities trade press — the exact readership that covers ABM's end market — reported the 30bp drop to 18.3%, the 16% leasing gain and the above-2022 projection.
San Francisco posted 963,980 sq ft of net absorption but vacancy of 29.2%, i.e. still roughly the multiple of New York the ABM CEO described.
The San Francisco office recovery on tech demand was written up in the real-estate trade press five days before the print.

verdicts.baseline_evidence: No move in the tape around 2026-07-29 or 2026-08-04 that I can attribute to this, and spot is -3.07% over 20 days — which argues the office recovery is not being paid for. But the segment it would flow to, B&I, has an already-disclosed company-specific headwind (TfL exit) that management pre-announced on 2026-06-05, the day the stock rose 6.67%. Truist's 2026-07-02 upgrade to Buy with a $58 target shows the thin coverage does still revise, so a published macro tailwind has had a transmission channel.
verdicts.what_would_change_it: Evidence that ABM's office janitorial revenue responds to net absorption within one or two quarters rather than after tenant build-out, or a B&I organic growth reacceleration that outweighs the disclosed TfL headwind.

verdicts.strongest_argument: Factually clean — I verified American's 2026-07-23 cut to -$0.65/+$0.65 from -$0.40/+$1.10 on ~$3.75/gal, Southwest's cut to $3.25-$4.25 from 'at least $4' after a ~$900m y/y Q2 fuel increase, and that Alaska suspended full-year guidance in April. But these are not obscure: they are among the most heavily covered corporate events of the summer, and the market's own verdict is on the record — American's stock rose 6.8% the day after it cut, because the fuel shock was already discounted in the airlines themselves. A second-order read-through to a ground-services vendor is strictly less informative than the first-order print that the market shrugged off. On transmission the claim runs the wrong way. Airline pain here is cost, not volume: American's Q2 revenue was +16.3% and Southwest's +20.3%, both records, and ABM's revenue is throughput-driven — management cited TSA throughput near 3m/day and robust leisure demand. ABM Aviation's growth drivers are airport-authority contracts, not airline-funded ones: LaGuardia Terminal B, Heathrow, Orlando International, Miami International. Vendor price pressure from airlines operates on renewal cycles, not inside a single quarter. And the qualitative warning is the company's own, published 2026-06-05 — the day the stock rose 6.67%, so it was not read as a reason to sell. The genuine Aviation risk is margin (6.3% to 5.3% on weather, contract scope changes and TSA-driven disruption), which is company-specific and orthogonal to jet fuel, and which the sell-side preview has already named as the central question for this print.

prior_publication.what_it_says: American cut FY26 to -$0.65/+$0.65 on ~$3.75/gal fuel, Southwest to $3.25-$4.25 from at least $4, and Alaska had suspended guidance in April.
American Airlines cut full-year guidance and the stock rose 6.8% the next day — the market treated the fuel shock as already priced.
American's first 2026 guidance cut on jet fuel came in April, i.e. before ABM's CEO gave the warning the claim treats as the starting point.
The published Q3 preview frames the print entirely around whether ABM can deliver the margin improvement 'that eluded it last quarter', with consensus at EPS $1.04 on revenue of $2.32bn.

verdicts.baseline_evidence: Spot -3.07% over 20 days and -4.68% from the 52-week high is consistent with some drift on soft second-order news, and the reaction history is 3-up/4-down with a 6.67% median, so downside is not unusual for this name. I cannot read the skew: 25-delta skew is null in the baseline and total front-expiry OI is 93 contracts with a 78%-of-mid ATM spread, so the 1.32 put/call OI ratio and the 8.13% implied move carry no information about positioning. Any argument that puts are or are not bid here is unavailable.
verdicts.what_would_change_it: A specific ABM airline contract repricing, scope reduction or lost station announced since 2026-06-05, or evidence that airline-funded work rather than airport-authority work drives the 19.5% Aviation growth.

verdicts.strongest_argument: Every element is factually correct and I want to say that plainly: the $(22.2)m pre-tax Q4 FY25 hit, the ~100bp adjusted EBITDA margin effect and the $(0.26)/sh are in ABM's own Q4 FY25 release; the SEC did force ABM to stop excluding prior-year self-insurance adjustments from adjusted EPS; and the FY26 range genuinely is stated 'before any impact from prior-year self-insurance adjustments', so the apparent inconsistency the claim flags is a real inconsistency in ABM's own disclosure, not a misread. It is nonetheless the most priced item in the brief, for two reasons. First, publication: the Note 8 language, the definition change and the guidance footnote were all filed on 2026-06-05, and the CFO spent time on the Q2 call saying the change 'de-risked Q4' and gave 'greater predictability and transparency', while the Q2/Q4 actuarial-review cadence is repeated boilerplate across years of ABM 10-Ks and 10-Ks. Second and fatally, the claim's conclusion is the default modelling assumption rather than a deviation from it: nobody's Q3 estimate contains a prior-year reserve charge, so its absence is worth nothing. It also creates no year-over-year delta — Q3 FY25 adjusted net income of $51.7m (~$0.82/sh) was struck on the old, self-insurance-excluding basis, and the $1.04 consensus against 26.8% growth is being compared to exactly that $0.82, so the comp is already clean of this item on both sides. Arithmetically the claim proves that a $0.00 line stays $0.00.

prior_publication.what_it_says: Q1 FY26 release states the FY26 adjusted EPS range of $3.85-$4.15 'before any impact from prior-year self-insurance adjustments' and discloses that after SEC communications ABM revised its non-GAAP definitions to no longer exclude prior-year self-insurance adjustments.
Q4 FY25 release quantifies the prior-year self-insurance adjustment at $(22.2)m pre-tax, ~100bp of adjusted EBITDA margin and $(0.26) of adjusted EPS.

Management explained on the Q2 FY26 call that prior-year self-insurance adjustments are now inside the guidance range, that this 'de-risked Q4', and listed the claims-handling programmes put in place after the ~$23m prior-year hit.
Q3 FY25 adjusted net income of $51.7m — roughly $0.82/sh — is the comp the $1.04 consensus is measured against, struck on the pre-restatement basis.

verdicts.baseline_evidence: The 2026-06-05 print, which carried this disclosure, produced +6.67% — the single largest up-reaction in seven events. Whatever relief value the insurance change had was paid for on that date. Nothing in the subsequent tape (-0.32% over 5 days, -3.07% over 20) is attributable to it, which is consistent with it being fully absorbed rather than pending.
verdicts.what_would_change_it: Evidence that any of the three published Q3 estimates actually embeds a prior-year self-insurance charge, or that ABM reviews a material minority of casualty programmes in Q3, would turn this from a restatement of the base case into a genuine variance.

interactions: Three of the four findings rest on the same document set filed 2026-06-05 — the Q2 FY26 press release, the 10-Q and the earnings call. ABM#3 cites the 10-Q Note 8 and the guidance footnote from it; ABM#1 and ABM#2 both build on CEO quotes from the same call. That is the date the stock rose 6.67%, the largest up-move in the seven-event history, so anything traceable to that package has been paid for once already and none of these three is independent of the others. ABM#0 and ABM#1 are structurally the same claim — post-guide third-party industry data confirming a trend management had itself already described on 2026-06-05, with a lagged and diluted transmission to reported revenue — so they should not be counted as two separate edges. ABM#0 also contradicts itself against the published Q3 preview: management said BESS projects are equipment-heavy and margin-compressed, and the whole sell-side question for this print is margin recovery, so a record installation quarter is a revenue positive and an EPS/mix negative, leaving the bullish sign unresolved. ABM#1 (bullish, B&I office) and ABM#2 (bearish, Aviation) point opposite ways on segment mix and largely net out at the total-company level; both segments also carry larger company-specific offsets already disclosed on 2026-06-05 — the ~300bp TfL exit headwind in B&I and the 6.3%-to-5.3% Aviation margin compression on weather, scope and TSA disruption — which dominate the macro signals the claims rely on. Finally, no verdict here uses the option chain: 93 contracts of front-expiry OI, a null 25-delta skew and a 78%-of-mid ATM spread mean the 8.13% implied move is not a statement of what the market priced, and I have treated it as unusable in both directions.
